content: Two authors independently reviewed the titles and abstracts of the studies. One author conducted a full-text review, while another extracted the relevant data. Two authors independently evaluated the risk of bias in the studies. Individual-level participant data were harmonized and analyzed at the study level. Physical activity data were categorized into quartiles at the study level, and study-specific associations with all-cause mortality were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards regression models. The results from individual studies were summarized using random-effects meta-analysis. The primary outcome measure was all-cause mortality. Data on physical activity, regardless of intensity, demonstrated an association with a lower risk of mortality, following a non-linear dose-response relationship. Higher levels of total physical activity, at any intensity, and reduced sedentary time were associated with a significantly lower risk of premature mortality. This relationship was particularly evident in middle-aged and older adults, with a non-linear dose-response pattern. Nine studies provided data on sitting time and cardiovascular disease (CVD) and cancer mortality, while five studies provided data on TV-viewing time and CVD and cancer mortality. A significant association between sedentary behavior and CVD mortality was observed in the least active quartile of physical activity. However, this association was less consistent in the second and third quartiles of physical activity, and no increased risk of CVD mortality was observed with increasing sedentary behavior in the most active quartile. Associations between sedentary behavior and cancer mortality were generally weaker, with a 6–21% higher risk observed only in the least active quartile of physical activity. Physical activity was found to modify the associations between sedentary behavior and both CVD and cancer mortality. These findings underscore the importance of engaging in higher volumes of moderate and vigorous physical activity to mitigate or eliminate the risks associated with prolonged sedentary behavior, particularly for individuals with high levels of daily sitting. A meta-analysis of studies examining daily sedentary time (ST) and all-cause mortality revealed a log-linear dose-response relationship. Higher amounts of daily sedentary time were associated with increased mortality risks. The cut-off for daily sedentary time was 7 hours per day in studies using self-reported data and 9 hours per day in studies using device-based measures. These findings suggest that higher daily sedentary time is log-linearly associated with increased all-cause mortality risk in adults. In older adults, a meta-analysis of studies examining objectively assessed daily sedentary time and all-cause mortality found a log-linear dose-response relationship. Increased mortality risks became significant when total sedentary time exceeded approximately 9 hours per day. These findings suggest that older adults should aim to reduce daily sitting time to lower mortality risks. Physical activity was associated with a reduced risk of colorectal cancer, with evidence suggesting that promoting physical activity during transport and reducing sedentary behavior in the workplace may be effective strategies for colorectal cancer prevention. A systematic review and meta-analysis reported a 23% lower relative risk of any type of colorectal neoplasia and a 27% lower risk of advanced colorectal neoplasia in individuals with the highest levels of physical activity compared to those with the lowest levels. Independent of physical activity, total sitting time and TV-viewing time were associated with greater risks for several major chronic disease outcomes, including all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality. A threshold of 6–8 hours per day of total sitting and 3–4 hours per day of TV viewing was identified, above which the risk of mortality increased. These findings highlight the importance of reducing sedentary behavior to improve health outcomes. In summary, higher levels of physical activity, regardless of intensity, and reduced sedentary time are associated with lower risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and other chronic disease outcomes. These findings emphasize the critical role of physical activity in mitigating the adverse health effects of prolonged sedentary behavior.
